title: Founded Apple Computer in the family garage with Steve Wozniak
statement: Co-founded Apple Computer Company with Steve Wozniak on April 1, 1976, in the Jobs family home on Crist Drive in Los Altos, funding the first Apple I boards by selling Wozniak's HP calculator and Jobs's Volkswagen van.
outcome: Roughly 200 Apple I units were built after retailer Paul Terrell ordered fifty assembled machines at $500 each; the April 1977 Apple II became one of the first highly successful mass-produced microcomputers, and Jobs was worth an estimated $250 million by age 25.

title: Launched the Macintosh with the Ridley Scott '1984' Super Bowl commercial
statement: Introduced the Macintosh on January 24, 1984, at the Flint Auditorium shareholders meeting, two days after airing the Ridley Scott-directed '1984' commercial during Super Bowl XVIII.
outcome: The first mass-produced computer with a graphical user interface and mouse, priced at $2,495, opened sluggishly before the LaserWriter and PageMaker made it the platform of the desktop publishing industry; the ad itself was ranked the greatest commercial by Advertising Age.

title: Resigned from Apple after losing the power struggle with John Sculley
statement: Submitted his resignation to Apple's board on September 17, 1985, after Sculley's reorganization plan stripped him of the Macintosh group and Jobs's counter-plot to remove Sculley leaked.
outcome: Five senior Apple employees resigned to join him; the twelve-year exile produced NeXT and Pixar, and the operating system Apple bought back in 1996 became the foundation of Mac OS X and iOS.

title: Founded NeXT after the Apple ouster
statement: Founded NeXT, Inc. with $7 million of his own money in 1985 to build workstations for higher education and business, later attracting heavy investment from Ross Perot.
outcome: NeXT sold only about 50,000 machines and exited hardware in 1993, but its NeXTSTEP environment hosted Tim Berners-Lee's invention of the World Wide Web at CERN and became the software foundation of every Apple operating system after 1997.

title: Bought Pixar out of Lucasfilm for $10 million
statement: Paid $5 million to George Lucas's Lucasfilm for the technology rights of its computer graphics division and invested $5 million of capital on February 3, 1986, taking the chairmanship of the spinout renamed Pixar.
outcome: After cumulative investments reaching $50 million and a $26 million three-film Disney deal, Toy Story's 1995 success and Pixar's IPO converted the bet into a public studio; Disney acquired Pixar for $7.4 billion in 2006, making Jobs Disney's largest individual shareholder with a board seat.

title: Returned to Apple through the NeXT acquisition and took the Microsoft deal
statement: Sold NeXT to Apple for roughly $429 million plus 1.5 million shares, announced December 20, 1996, then as interim chief executive announced the August 1997 Microsoft partnership — $150 million invested, a five-year Office for Mac commitment, and a patent settlement — at Macworld Boston.
outcome: Jobs cut the product sprawl, ended Mac cloning, and shipped the 1998 iMac; Apple went from a $2.46 billion market capitalization at the deal's announcement to overtaking Microsoft in market value by May 26, 2010.

title: Entered the phone business with the multi-touch iPhone
statement: Introduced the iPhone on January 9, 2007, at Macworld in San Francisco as a widescreen iPod, a phone, and an internet communicator in one, built through a secret $150 million collaboration with Cingular and released June 29, 2007 at $499 and $599.
outcome: Six of ten Americans knew of the launch beforehand, stores sold out within an hour, Time named it Invention of the Year, and the iPhone propelled Apple past Microsoft in market value by 2010 and into the ranks of the world's most profitable companies.

title: Created the tablet category with the iPad
statement: Introduced the iPad on January 27, 2010, an iOS-based tablet built around a multi-touch screen with a virtual keyboard, with retail availability beginning that April.
outcome: Rather than cannibalizing the Mac, iPad sales produced a halo effect that lifted iMac and MacBook demand, and more than 250 million iPads had been sold by April 2015.

title: Resigned as chief executive and named Tim Cook his successor
statement: Announced his resignation as Apple's chief executive on August 24, 2011, telling the board that the day he could no longer meet his duties and expectations had come, becoming chairman and recommending Tim Cook as successor.
outcome: Jobs worked for Apple until the day before his death on October 5, 2011, from respiratory arrest following a relapse of his pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor; Cook's Apple went on to become the world's most valuable company, and Jobs was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2022.
